# Working With AI Coding Tools and Still Owning the Result

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against METR's 2025 study and February 2026 update, the Peng, Perry and Spracklen papers (full text), DORA's 2025 report page and Claude Code's best-practices and memory docs. The can-it-fail demo was re-run.

Starts from: lessons 01 and 02 (the feedback loop; specs with executable criteria).

## The problem and why it matters

An AI coding tool (an *agent* that reads your repository, edits files and runs commands from a plain-language request) hands you a 600-line change in two minutes. A reviewer asks, "why does this take a lock here?" If you cannot answer, you have not shipped your work; you have forwarded someone else's. When it breaks at night, the pager is yours.

The bar a senior engineering role will hold you to is simple: **you can explain, validate, debug and modify any code the tool wrote**. The tool changes how fast code appears, not who is accountable.

## First principles

1. **Plausible is not correct.** A language model produces text that looks like good code, so verification has to come from outside it: running the code, tests, type checks, reading.
2. **The agent stops when the work looks done.** Anthropic's Claude Code best-practices page says that if it has nothing to run that tells it whether the work is done, "looks done" is all it has, and you become the test suite. Give it a check to run and ask for evidence (command and output), not "all tests pass".
3. **Review capacity is the bottleneck, so diffs must be small.** A *diff* is the set of lines a change adds and removes. Careful review of 600 lines is hard (my experience, not a measured result). One task, one small diff.
4. **Tests are the contract, so the tool may not weaken them.** The failure is silent: a test goes red, the tool edits the test, CI goes green. Treat any change to a test as a change to the requirements.
5. **Instructions are context, not enforcement.** Claude Code treats `CLAUDE.md` as "context, not enforced configuration"; must-not-happen rules belong in CI, hooks and permissions.
6. **The evidence on productivity is mixed.** See below.

## How it works

### The routine

```
 spec + plan                       (you)
      │
      ▼
 ┌─▶ one small task ──▶ failing test (red)
 │                            │
 │                            ▼
 │                     tool implements
 │                            │
 │                            ▼
 │                you RUN it, read the diff
 │                  with the checklist below
 │                            │
 └──────── small commit ◀─────┘  (or reject)
```

### Ladder of evidence

```
 weakest
  "the tool says it works"
  "tests pass"
  "tests pass AND can fail"   (mutation check)
  "I ran it on real input"
  "I can explain every changed line"
 strongest   (gated work needs the whole ladder)
```

### What the research says

- **Strong design, narrow scope.** METR ran a randomized controlled trial: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 real issues in repositories they knew, each issue randomly allowed or disallowed AI (the repositories averaged over 1M lines of code and 22k stars). Result, in its words: developers "take 19% longer than without". They had expected a 24% speed-up and afterward still believed AI had sped them up by 20%. The authors call it "a snapshot of early-2025 AI capabilities in one relevant setting", not evidence about most developers. The 2025 post now says its results no longer reflect current tools. In February 2026 METR called its follow-up data "an unreliable signal" (more developers declined to take part because they did not want to work without AI; time measurements were unreliable for developers running several agents at once) and offered only "very weak evidence" on the current size of any speed-up.
- **Conflicting result, different task.** Peng et al. ran a controlled experiment where developers implemented an HTTP server in JavaScript: the Copilot group "completed the task 55.8% faster" (95% confidence interval 21-89%). The 2022 experiment recruited 95 freelancers through Upwork, and 35 completed the task and survey. One self-contained task is not a mature codebase.
- **Quality and security.** In a user study of 47 participants on five security-related tasks, Perry et al. found participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to believe it was secure. Spracklen et al. generated 576,000 code samples (Python and JavaScript, 16 models) and found hallucinated package names (names that do not exist) on average "at least 5.2%" of the time for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, in their setup.
- **Organizational.** DORA's 2025 report page says AI's "primary role is as an amplifier" of an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses (that one sentence is from the report's summary page; I did not read the report's findings).

Summary: results conflict, tasks differ, and people misjudge their own speed. Treat generated code like human code that needs the checks, and the rest as anecdote.

### Practices

- **Plan, then test, then code.** Read and fix the plan first; approve failing tests; tell the tool "do not edit the tests".
- **Scope each task:** name the files, the behavior and the stopping condition.
- **Context hygiene.** Commands, conventions and boundaries go in a short instruction file (Claude Code's docs suggest under about 200 lines); fresh session per task; no secrets or customer data in prompts.
- **Run it yourself** on real input before trusting a green test run.
- **Disclose.** Follow employer policy; note assistance in the PR or a commit trailer; keep README claims accurate.

### When not to use the tool

When you cannot judge the output (security-critical code); when the spec is unclear (explore by hand first); when verifying costs more than writing; to learn a skill; for a large refactor with no tests; when the data must not leave your machine.

### Review checklist for an AI-written diff (copy it)

```markdown
- [ ] I can explain every changed line, including why this approach.
- [ ] Diff is small and on-task; no unrelated edits, renames or reformatting.
- [ ] No test was weakened, skipped or deleted; assertion changes explained.
- [ ] New tests failed before the change (saw red) and can fail (mutation check).
- [ ] I ran it on real input myself, not only the test suite.
- [ ] Every new API, flag and package exists in the version we use (checked docs or the type checker).
- [ ] New dependencies: real, maintained, needed; lockfile diff reviewed.
- [ ] No secrets, tokens or keys in code, logs or prompts; errors handled at boundaries.
- [ ] Shell commands and migrations read before running.
- [ ] Spec/ADR updated if behavior or a decision changed; AI assistance noted per policy.
```

### Failure modes

| Failure | How it looks | Catch it with |
|---|---|---|
| Hallucinated API | Plausible method that does not exist | Type checker, run it, read the docs |
| Confident wrong fix | Explains a cause it never reproduced | Reproduce first; failing test before fix |
| Sprawling change | Touches 30 files for a 3-line fix | Scoped task; reject large diffs |
| Silent test weakening | Assertion loosened, test skipped | Diff the tests; CI rule for test changes |
| Outdated library usage | Deprecated call from old training data | Check lockfile version against docs |

### Runnable demo: a weak test passes while the code is wrong

`pricing.py` has a bug (it subtracts the percent as if it were money):

```python
def apply_discount(price, percent):
    """Return price after taking `percent` percent off. 0 <= percent <= 100."""
    return price - percent          # BUG
```

A hurried assistant writes tests that assert something sensible (`test_weak.py`): `apply_discount(200, 0) == 200`, the result is a number, and the result is `<= 200`. All three pass on the bug:

```text
...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.00s
```

The "can it fail?" check swaps in hand-written wrong versions and sees which the suite misses:

```python
# check_can_fail.py  usage: python check_can_fail.py test_weak.py
import subprocess, sys, pathlib, shutil, tempfile
GUARD = "if not 0 <= percent <= 100:\n        raise ValueError(percent)\n    "
VERSIONS = {            # name: (body, is_correct)
    "returns price unchanged":    (GUARD + "return price", False),
    "subtracts percent as money": (GUARD + "return price - percent", False),
    "returns the discount":       (GUARD + "return price * percent / 100", False),
    "adds instead of subtracting": (GUARD + "return price * (1 + percent / 100)", False),
    "no range check":             ("return price * (1 - percent / 100)", False),
    "CORRECT version":            (GUARD + "return price * (1 - percent / 100)", True),
}
suite = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
for name, (body, correct) in VERSIONS.items():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        shutil.copy(suite, d)
        pathlib.Path(d, "pricing.py").write_text(
            "def apply_discount(price, percent):\n    " + body + "\n")
        r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-x", "-p", "no:cacheprovider",
                            suite.name], cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True)
        passed = r.returncode == 0
        verdict = ("ok: passes the correct code" if passed else "BAD: fails correct code") if correct \
            else ("MISSED: wrong code passes" if passed else "caught")
        print(f"{name:<28} -> {verdict}")
```

Captured here on macOS for `test_weak.py`, then for a stronger suite that asserts known answers (`(200,10)->180`, `(80,25)->60`, `(200,100)->0`) and that 101 and -1 raise `ValueError`:

```text
=== weak
returns price unchanged      -> MISSED: wrong code passes
subtracts percent as money   -> MISSED: wrong code passes
returns the discount         -> caught
adds instead of subtracting  -> caught
no range check               -> MISSED: wrong code passes
CORRECT version              -> ok: passes the correct code
=== strong
returns price unchanged      -> caught
subtracts percent as money   -> caught
returns the discount         -> caught
adds instead of subtracting  -> caught
no range check               -> caught
CORRECT version              -> ok: passes the correct code
```

Both pass on the correct version, so green cannot tell them apart. Only the check exposes the weak one.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a bug fix lands with green CI; two days later the bug is back in production.

1. **Reproduce** with the incident's real input. It still fails.
2. **Read the PR's test diff.** The tool's first run was red; its "fix" changed the expected value to match the output.
3. **Check the rest of the PR** for other loosened assertions. Two more.
4. **Fix:** restore the original assertions, confirm they fail, then fix the code.
5. **Prevent:** call out test-file changes in the PR template, flag edits to existing assertions in CI, and run the can-it-fail check on AI-written tests.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Boilerplate, glue, tests for known behavior, mechanical migrations | Security-critical code you cannot judge |
| Exploring an unfamiliar codebase | You would accept its answer unchecked |
| A failing test and a small scope | A vague spec and a large diff |

## Interview questions

1. How do you use AI tools without lowering quality? *Outline:* plan, small tasks, tests first, run it, checklist, own every line.
2. A tool says "done, tests pass". What do you do? *Probe:* what if it edited the tests? *Outline:* read the test diff; ask for command output; run it yourself.
3. What does the research say about AI productivity? *Outline:* mixed: METR (slower, mature repos, early 2025) versus faster on a self-contained task; both with caveats.
4. What are hallucinated packages and why do they matter? *Outline:* nonexistent names; supply-chain risk; verify every dependency.
5. When would you not use the tool? *Outline:* unjudgeable output, unclear spec, learning, sensitive data.

**Exercise (do it):** take one small function in your own repo. Ask a tool to write tests for it. Write three wrong versions by hand and run the can-it-fail check. Count the MISSED. Ask the tool to strengthen the tests only, rerun, and review with the checklist. Note the before and after counts.

## Checklist

1. I can state the bar: explain, validate, debug, modify.
2. I work in small, test-first tasks and ask for command output.
3. I review AI diffs with a written checklist and read the test diff first.
4. I know the research is mixed and can name two studies with their caveats.
5. I never paste secrets, and I verify every new dependency.

## Common wrong answers

- "The tests pass, so it is correct." Weak tests pass on wrong code.
- "The AI wrote it, so it's the AI's bug." You merged it.
- "Longer prompts fix hallucination." Checks catch it.
- "Studies prove AI makes developers faster (or slower)." Each is one setting.
- "`CLAUDE.md` forbids it, so it cannot happen." It is context, not enforcement.
